WATCH: A police patrolman has sustained a skull and wrist injury after supposedly being punched in the head by an individual at a Labor Day rally along Kalaw Avenue in Manila on Friday, May 1.

PNP spokesperson BGen. Randulf Tuaño claims the individual who purportedly punched the police officer was a member of the groups leading the protest.

Sectoral groups mounted the rally on Friday to call for an end for the US-Israel war against Iran and to hold President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. accountable for supposedly failing to address demands for higher wages and lower costs of basic goods. | @jasonsigalesINQ

data.text:
Dewey's Beatdown
MANILA BAY
May 1 1898

The Spanish American War became a two-ocean naval war. For once America was prepared. Her navy was three times as large as Spain's and far more efficient. The American Navy had four first-class battleships against Spain's one, which was in drydock. Her cruisers and other warships were vastly better equipped and served than those of the Spanish Navy.

Never before or since has the American Navy sailed into battle with such superiority and much of this was due to the theories of Captain MaHan and the driving energy of Theodore Roosevelt, Assistant Secretary of the Navy.

Rear Admiral Patrico Pasaron, commander of the Spanish squadron in Manila Bay, was like most Spanish officers; utterly brave and utterly defeatist. To prevent the bombardment of Manila, he stationed his seven ships in shallow waters. There, in gloomy resolution, he awaited the Americans.

Commadore Dewey quickly cleared his decks for battle. The seven Spanish ships were in line. The Spanish fleet fired first, wild and high. At that Commadore Dewey said, "You may fire when ready." At a distance of 5,500 yards, Olympia's 8-incher belched smoke and flame. Soon all American ships were firing, deliberately with slow majesty. Dewy paraded his bellowing ships before the Spanish ships. Five times they promenaded, three times west and twice east, until the smoke of battle obscured the stricken enemy.

Dewey broke off the action for breakfast. At 11:16 AM, Dewy stood ready to renew the battle. By then the Spanish fleet was dying, it was a blazing shambles.

It was all over. Dewey's squadron took up unchallenged command of the bay, masters of Manila and of the entire Philippine Archipelago as well.
 In seven hours, with not a man killed and only eight slightly wounded, the United States had become a world power!
